# Several experiments on LLMs, places, names, and race

## Model runs on names and places

Last week's results included evidence that `gemma-2-9b` can partially recreate a
measure similar to the name component of BISFG. This week, I'm looking if the
location component.

One caveat here is that BISFG would use tract or even block level data to come
up with a very precise race proportion for a given address, and we're using city
(Census place) because I'm not currently generating real addresses.

Possibly, we can add neighborhood to the data generation, using Detroit as the
first case. More work to be done here!

#### Avoiding reporting the linear model's 'memorization' of the dataset - LATER

I had meant to spend some time working with the paper, "Designing and
Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks," before. Since this is a linear probe
essentially that I'm building to try and understand the model encoding of race,
it was as good a time as any to try and develop this model against a control
task.

They talk about the goal to build *selective* probes. Selective probes achieve
"high linguistic task accuracy and low control task accuracy." 

They also refer to random representation baselines.

This is a line to check out later: "as long as a representation is a lossless
encoding, a sufficiently expressive probe with enough training data can learn
*any* task on top of it."
- TODO: Are the tokenization and vectorization schemes, even if they're only the
  randomly initialized vectors, a lossless encoding? Maybe? The n dimension of
  the vector though is << the vocabulary size typically. Does that matter? The
  vector length of models if you treated them as bits could certainly hold the
  vocab size. So maybe yeah.

So far I've focused on simple linear probes, but they echo an argument for 
'complex,' probes because the characteristics you're interested in my not be
encoded linearly. They do show that MLPs tend to be less selective.

They mention using @marcusmitchellp.Treebank31999 for their dependency edge
prediction task.

They also talk about using an LR decomposition to further constrain the linear 
model -- this is interesting. How could this work in conjunction with PCA or
something like that?

Has selectivity been researched in semantic tasks? Maybe, maybe not -- the work
has been cited at least.

## The 'Approve - Review' task

- [ ] Write the prompt
- [ ] Run the challenge using white as a baseline
- [ ] Run the challenge using ambiguous names as a baseline

The problem with the full 'order candidates' mortgage application task is that
it is a fairly complicated task, so applying interpretability techniques gets
intractable fast. This task draws from a similar dataset as that task but
instead looks at one candidate at a time, asking the model to approve or review.

I did two versions of this experiment with different baselines, one using a
signaled white candidates, and one using an intentionally ambiguous candidates
under BISFG.

In this task, I'm starting at the logits for the 'approve' and 'review,' tokens
then looking at how the name and place contributes.
